bottom_line: A competent, conventionally structured Express + Postgres order service whose real ceiling is that every request path still goes through one 900-line controller layer with no transaction boundary, so correctness under concurrency is asserted in code review rather than enforced by the database.

top_fixes.title: Wrap order creation and stock decrement in one transaction
top_fixes.why: Two sequential writes with no transaction: an insert into orders followed by a stock decrement. A crash or a rejected decrement between them leaves a paid order with stock never reserved, and two concurrent buyers can both pass the availability check.
top_fixes.fix: Move both writes inside a single prisma.$transaction, and make the decrement conditional (UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= qty) so the database, not the request handler, is what prevents overselling.

top_fixes.title: Stop logging the full Stripe webhook body
top_fixes.why: The raw webhook payload is written to the application log at info level. It carries customer email, billing address and the payment-method fingerprint, so PII lands in log storage that has a different retention policy and a much wider read audience than the database.
top_fixes.fix: Log event.id and event.type only. If the body is needed for debugging, put it behind a flag that is off in production and redact customer and payment_method before writing.

top_fixes.title: Add the composite index the order-history query actually needs
top_fixes.why: The customer order-history query filters on customer_id and sorts by created_at, but only customer_id is indexed, so Postgres sorts the whole matching set on every call. It is the second most-called endpoint and the cost grows with each customer's history.
top_fixes.fix: Add a composite index on (customer_id, created_at DESC) and confirm with EXPLAIN that the sort disappears from the plan.

top_fixes.title: Cover the refund path before touching it again
top_fixes.why: The refund service moves money and has zero tests, while being the third most-changed file in the last 90 days. Every change to it is currently validated by review alone.
top_fixes.fix: Start with the three branches that decide an amount: full refund, partial refund, and an already-refunded order. A fake Stripe client is enough - the point is the arithmetic and the guard, not the network call.

top_fixes.title: Fail the build when a migration is missing
top_fixes.why: CI runs the test suite against a database built from migrations, but nothing checks that the Prisma schema and the migration history agree. A schema edit committed without its migration passes CI and fails at deploy time instead.
top_fixes.fix: Add `npx prisma migrate diff --from-migrations ./prisma/migrations --to-schema-datamodel ./prisma/schema.prisma --exit-code` as a CI step; a non-zero exit means a migration is missing.

architect.summary: A conventional three-layer Express service - routes, controllers, repositories - with Prisma as the only data access path and Redis used purely as a cache aside. The layering is real and mostly respected, but the controller layer has absorbed business logic that belongs in services, and there is no transaction boundary anywhere in the write path, so invariants that span two tables are enforced by convention rather than by the database.
points: Every HTTP route is a thin binding: `src/routes/orders.ts:12` maps the verb to a controller method and does nothing else, so routing can be read in one file.

All database access funnels through `src/repositories/`; no controller imports the Prisma client directly (`src/repositories/order.repo.ts:1` is the only place `new PrismaClient` appears), which is what makes the data layer swappable at all.

The controller layer is where the design slips: `src/controllers/orders.controller.ts` is 902 lines and holds pricing, stock and fulfilment decisions that the empty `src/services/` directory was clearly meant to own.

No transaction boundary exists in the codebase - `grep -rn 'prisma.$transaction' src/` returns nothing - so any invariant spanning two tables (order + stock, refund + ledger) is only as strong as the ordering of two separate awaits.
Redis is a clean cache-aside at `src/cache/product.cache.ts:22`: read-through with a TTL, and every write path deletes the key rather than updating it, so a stale entry cannot outlive a change.
Error handling is centralised in one Express error middleware (`src/middleware/error.ts:18`) that maps a small set of domain errors to status codes - the single best structural decision in the repo.
The Stripe integration is the one place the layering is bypassed: `src/routes/webhooks.ts:44` reads and writes the database directly from the route, with no controller or repository in between.
table: HTTP surface: verb, path, auth middleware, and a controller call
Request handling plus, in practice, most business logic
Intended home for business logic - currently holds only refund.service.ts
The only Prisma access; one module per aggregate

infra.summary: Containerised, reproducible and deployed from CI on every merge to main, with a real Postgres service in the test job rather than a mock. Two gaps keep it off an A: nothing verifies that the Prisma schema and its migration history agree, so a missing migration fails at deploy rather than in CI, and the production image still runs as root.

findings.title: CI never checks that the schema and the migration history agree
findings.consequence: A schema change committed without its migration passes every CI gate and then fails at deploy, when the container starts against a database that does not have the column. The failure lands in production deploy logs instead of on the pull request.
findings.evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:31  run: npx prisma migrate deploy && npm test
prisma/migrations/  20 directories, newest 20260821_add_order_notes
No `migrate diff` or `--exit-code` anywhere in the workflow.
findings.fix: Add `npx prisma migrate diff --from-migrations ./prisma/migrations --to-schema-datamodel ./prisma/schema.prisma --exit-code` as its own step; non-zero means a migration is missing.

findings.title: The production container runs as root
findings.consequence: Any remote code execution in the Node process starts with uid 0 inside the container, which removes the last cheap barrier between an application bug and the container filesystem, including the mounted secrets directory.
findings.evidence:
Dockerfile:24  CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
No USER directive anywhere in the file; `docker run --rm orders-api id` prints uid=0(root).
findings.fix: Add `RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app` and `USER app` before CMD, and chown the app directory in the build stage.

findings.title: Health check reports the process, not its dependencies
findings.consequence: The endpoint returns 200 as long as Node is running, so an instance that has lost its database connection pool stays in the load balancer and keeps taking traffic it cannot serve.
findings.evidence:
src/routes/health.ts:9  res.json({ ok: true, uptime: process.uptime() })
No query, no Redis ping; the orchestrator's readiness probe points at this path.
findings.fix: Run `SELECT 1` and a Redis PING with a short timeout, and return 503 when either fails. Keep a separate liveness path that stays cheap.

findings.title: Secrets are read from the environment with no validation at boot
findings.consequence: A missing or misspelled variable surfaces as undefined deep in a request handler, typically as a confusing runtime error under load rather than a clear failure at startup.
findings.evidence:
src/config.ts:8  export const config = { databaseUrl: process.env.DATABASE_URL, stripeKey: process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY }
No throw, no schema, no default; both values flow onward as possibly-undefined.
findings.fix: Validate the whole environment once at boot with a schema and exit non-zero on a miss, so a misconfigured deploy fails immediately and visibly.

security.summary: Authentication and authorisation are handled consistently and the obvious injection surfaces are closed by Prisma's parameterisation, but the service leaks customer PII into application logs, trusts a webhook whose signature it verifies only when a secret happens to be set, and ships rate limiting that a single header can bypass. None of these need an attacker to be clever.

findings.title: The full Stripe webhook body is written to the application log
findings.consequence: Customer email, billing address and the payment-method fingerprint land in log storage, which has a longer retention and a far wider read audience than the database. It converts a payments integration into a PII exposure that no data-access review would catch.
findings.evidence:
src/routes/webhooks.ts:44  logger.info('stripe webhook', { body: req.body })
src/routes/webhooks.ts:51  const { customer_email, billing_details } = req.body.data.object;
findings.fix: Log `event.id` and `event.type` only. If the body is genuinely needed, put it behind a debug flag that is off in production and redact customer and payment_method first.

findings.title: Webhook signature verification is skipped when the secret is unset
findings.consequence: The verification branch is conditional on the environment variable being present, so an environment that is missing STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET accepts unsigned requests and processes them as real payment events. A misconfigured deploy silently becomes an unauthenticated write endpoint for orders.
findings.fix: Invert it: refuse to start without the secret, and reject every webhook request that fails verification. A missing secret is a deployment error, not a reason to trust the caller.

findings.title: Rate limiting keys on a client-supplied header
findings.consequence: The limiter buckets by X-Forwarded-For without a trusted-proxy configuration, so a caller that sets the header itself gets a fresh bucket per request and is never limited. The login and checkout paths that most need the protection are the ones that lose it.
findings.evidence:
src/middleware/rateLimit.ts:14  keyGenerator: (req) => req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] ?? req.ip,
src/server.ts:18  // app.set('trust proxy', ...) is commented out
findings.fix: Set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` for the real proxy hop and key on `req.ip`, which Express then derives from the trusted header rather than from whatever the client sent.

findings.title: Password reset tokens are generated with Math.random
findings.consequence: Math.random is not a cryptographic source and its output is predictable from a few observed values, so a reset token can be guessed rather than intercepted. The token is the only thing standing between a known email address and account takeover.
findings.evidence: src/services/refund.service.ts:8  const token = Math.random().toString(36).slice(2) + Date.now().toString(36);
findings.fix: Use `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')`, store only a hash of the token, and give it a short expiry.

findings.title: One dependency with a known high-severity advisory
findings.consequence: The advisory is a prototype-pollution issue in a transitive parser used on the request path, so it is reachable from unauthenticated input rather than only from build tooling.
findings.evidence:
npm audit --json  ->  "high": 1, "moderate": 3, "low": 5
The high advisory resolves to a transitive dependency of the body parsing stack; a patched version exists.
findings.fix: Run `npm audit fix`, confirm the tree no longer resolves the vulnerable version, and add `npm audit --audit-level=high` to CI so the next one fails the build.

performance.summary: Response times are fine at current volume, but three of the four hot paths do work that scales with data rather than with the request: an unindexed sort on order history, an N+1 on the order-lines join, and a cache that is invalidated correctly but never warmed, so every deploy starts with a thundering herd against Postgres.

findings.title: Order history sorts the whole result set on every request
findings.consequence: The query filters on customer_id and orders by created_at, but only customer_id is indexed, so Postgres reads every order for that customer and sorts them each time. Cost grows with a customer's lifetime history on the second most-called endpoint in the service.
findings.evidence:
src/repositories/order.repo.ts:96  where: { customerId }, orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }, take: 20
prisma/schema.prisma:61  @@index([customerId])
EXPLAIN shows a Sort node above an Index Scan, no index used for ordering.
findings.fix: Add `@@index([customerId, createdAt(sort: Desc)])` and confirm with EXPLAIN that the Sort node disappears.

findings.title: The order-list endpoint issues one query per order for its lines
findings.consequence: A page of 20 orders costs 21 round trips. The endpoint is called on every dashboard load, so the database sees twenty times the traffic it needs for the single most common read in the product.
findings.fix: Fetch the lines in one query with `include: { lines: true }`, or a single `findMany({ where: { orderId: { in: ids } } })` grouped in memory.

findings.title: The product cache is never warmed, so every deploy stampedes Postgres
findings.consequence: Cache-aside with a cold Redis means the first request for each product after a deploy goes to the database, and concurrent requests for the same key all miss together. The effect is a latency spike on every release rather than a steady state problem.
findings.evidence:
src/cache/product.cache.ts:22  const hit = await redis.get(key); if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit);
No single-flight guard, no warm-up on boot; the TTL is 300s so the pattern repeats.
findings.fix: Add a single-flight lock so concurrent misses for one key collapse into one query, and warm the top N products on boot.

findings.title: JSON responses are not compressed
findings.consequence: Order-list payloads run to hundreds of kilobytes and cross the network uncompressed, which is felt most by the mobile clients that can least afford it.
findings.evidence:
src/server.ts:24  app.use(express.json({ limit: '1mb' }));
No compression middleware is registered anywhere in the file.
findings.fix: Add the compression middleware ahead of the routes, or terminate compression at the proxy if one is already in front.

quality.summary: TypeScript is on with strict mode and the linter runs in CI, which puts a floor under the whole codebase. What holds it back is concentration: one controller holds a third of the application logic, error handling is duplicated in a dozen catch blocks that all do the same thing slightly differently, and 14 exported functions are never called.

findings.title: One controller holds a third of the application logic
findings.consequence: 902 lines mixing pricing, stock, fulfilment and response shaping. Two developers touching different features collide in the same file, and the empty services directory next to it shows where the code was meant to go.
findings.evidence:
src/controllers/orders.controller.ts  902 lines, 11 exported handlers
src/services/  contains only refund.service.ts
findings.fix: Lift the three clearest domains - pricing, stock, fulfilment - into services and leave the controller doing validation, delegation and response shaping.

findings.title: The same catch block is written twelve times
findings.consequence: Each copy logs and maps to a status code slightly differently, so the API's error shape depends on which handler failed. There is already a central error middleware that these bypass.
findings.evidence:
src/controllers/orders.controller.ts:88  } catch (e) { logger.error(e); res.status(500).json({ error: 'failed' }); }
The same three-line shape appears at :121, :167, :203, :244 and 7 more sites.
findings.fix: Delete the catch blocks and let the errors reach `src/middleware/error.ts:18`, which already maps domain errors to status codes. Wrap async handlers once so rejections get there.

findings.title: Fourteen exported functions are never called
findings.consequence: Dead code reads as API surface. A newcomer cannot tell which helpers are load-bearing, and the unused ones still get maintained through refactors.
findings.evidence:
src/utils/format.ts:12  export function formatLegacyOrderId(id: string)  - no importer
13 further exports across src/utils/ have no call site outside their own tests.
findings.fix: Delete them. Git remembers, and the ones that turn out to be needed come back with a caller attached.

findings.title: Magic numbers carry business meaning inline
findings.consequence: Thresholds that encode policy - free-shipping minimum, maximum line quantity, refund window - appear as bare numbers at their use sites, so changing a policy means grepping for a literal.
findings.evidence:
src/controllers/orders.controller.ts:312  if (subtotal > 5000) { shipping = 0; }
Similar literals at :330 (quantity cap 99) and src/services/refund.service.ts:41 (30-day window).
findings.fix: Move them into a named policy module so the rule is readable and changing it is a one-line edit with a test attached.

tests.summary: A real suite exists - 148 tests, Jest plus supertest, running in CI against a genuine Postgres service - and the paths it covers are covered properly. The problem is what it skips: the money paths. Refunds have no tests at all, the webhook handler is tested only for its happy path, and coverage is collected but never enforced, so it has drifted down for six months without failing anything.

findings.title: The refund service has no tests and is the third most-changed file
findings.consequence: Code that decides how much money to return to a customer is validated by review alone, and it changes often. A wrong branch here is a financial error, not a 500.
findings.evidence:
tests/  no file references refund.service
git log --format= --name-only --since=90.days | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn  ->  31 src/services/refund.service.ts
findings.fix: Cover the three branches that decide an amount: full refund, partial refund, and an already-refunded order. A fake Stripe client is enough - the arithmetic and the guard are the point.

findings.title: The webhook handler is tested only for the happy path
findings.consequence: The single test posts a correctly signed event and asserts a 200. Nothing asserts that an unsigned request is rejected, that a replayed event is idempotent, or that an unknown event type is ignored - and all three are reachable from the public internet.
findings.evidence:
tests/integration/webhooks.test.ts:18  it('accepts a signed checkout.session.completed', ...)
The file contains exactly one `it(`.
findings.fix: Add three cases: bad signature is 400, the same event id twice creates one order, an unknown type is a no-op 200.

findings.title: Coverage is measured but never enforced, and has fallen for six months
findings.consequence: A number nobody has to meet is a number that only moves one way. Coverage has dropped from 74% to 61% without a single build failing, so the decline was invisible until someone looked.
findings.evidence:
jest.config.js:14  collectCoverage: true,
No coverageThreshold key anywhere in the file; CI uploads the report and asserts nothing about it.
findings.fix: Set a coverageThreshold just under today's numbers and raise it whenever it is comfortably beaten. A ratchet stops the slide without blocking work.

findings.title: Integration tests share one database and depend on execution order
findings.consequence: Rows created by one test are visible to the next, so the suite passes in file order and fails when run with --shard or a single -t filter. It makes a failure hard to reproduce locally, which is exactly when reproduction matters.
findings.evidence:
tests/integration/setup.ts:7  beforeAll(async () => { await prisma.$executeRaw`TRUNCATE orders CASCADE` })
Truncation runs once per FILE, not per test; several tests assert on counts.
findings.fix: Truncate in beforeEach, or wrap each test in a transaction that is rolled back. Then a single test can run alone and still pass.

docs.summary: The README gets a new developer running - install, env, migrate, start, all accurate and verified by following them - and the OpenAPI spec is genuinely useful. Beyond that it thins out fast: the spec has drifted from the routes it documents, the architecture is explained nowhere, and three environment variables the service needs are documented only by their absence at boot.

findings.title: The OpenAPI spec is missing 13 routes and documents 2 that were removed
findings.consequence: Clients are generated from this file. A route that is absent gets no client method, and a route that no longer exists generates a method that 404s - both discovered by the consumer, at runtime.
findings.evidence:
openapi.yaml  31 paths
src/routes/  44 registered routes
openapi.yaml:302  /orders/{id}/legacy-invoice  - no matching route in src/routes/
findings.fix: Generate the spec from the route definitions, or add a CI check that compares the two lists and fails on a difference.

findings.title: Three required environment variables are undocumented
findings.consequence: A new environment starts, passes its health check, and then fails on the first webhook or the first cache read. The missing variables are discovered one incident at a time.
findings.evidence:
README.md:61  documents 9 variables
src/config.ts reads 12; REDIS_TLS_URL, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET and ORDER_EXPORT_BUCKET appear in neither the README nor .env.example.
findings.fix: Regenerate the table from `src/config.ts` and add a `.env.example` with every key present and every secret blank.

findings.title: Nothing explains how the service is put together
findings.consequence: The layering, the transaction rules and the cache invalidation contract exist only in the code and in the heads of the two people who wrote it. Onboarding is a week of reading instead of an afternoon.
findings.evidence:
README.md  184 lines: install, env, scripts, deploy. No architecture section.
docs/  does not exist.
findings.fix: One page: the layer diagram, where business logic belongs, the cache invalidation rule, and the transaction rule. It pays for itself with the second hire.

findings.title: The README's test command has drifted
findings.consequence: The documented command fails for anyone who follows it, which is a bad first ten minutes and a wholly avoidable one.
findings.evidence:
README.md:122  npm run test:all
package.json:18  scripts has test, test:unit, test:int - no test:all
findings.fix: Point it at `npm test`, and add a CI step that runs every command the README documents.

uiux.summary: Backend service with no user-facing surface - no templates, no static assets, no client. This lens is omitted from the report and from the overall score.

features.summary: A coherent order lifecycle - cart, checkout, payment, fulfilment, refund - with nothing half-built in the main path. The edges are where it frays: bulk export is behind a flag that has been on in production for five months, and the loyalty module is fully implemented but has no route reaching it.

children.name: Pricing rules
children.note: in the controller, not a service

children.name: Bulk export
children.note: behind a flag that has been on for 5 months

good: One centralised error middleware (src/middleware/error.ts:18) maps domain errors to status codes, so the API's error shape is a deliberate design rather than an accident of which handler failed.
Every database call goes through src/repositories/ - `new PrismaClient` appears exactly once, at src/repositories/order.repo.ts:1 - which is what makes the data layer testable and swappable at all.
CI runs against a real postgres:16 service (.github/workflows/ci.yml:14) instead of a mock, so the integration tests exercise genuine SQL, genuine constraints and genuine migration state.
TypeScript strict mode is on and has never been turned off for a file (tsconfig.json:7, zero @ts-ignore in src/), which is rarer than it should be and is doing quiet work throughout.
Cache invalidation is correct by construction: every write path deletes the key rather than updating it (src/cache/product.cache.ts:41), so a stale entry cannot outlive a change.
bad: scripts/seed-dev.js:12 connects with the production DATABASE_URL when NODE_ENV is unset, and the README tells new developers to run it before setting anything.
The Dockerfile installs devDependencies into the runtime image (Dockerfile:11), which is most of the 412 MB and every one of their advisories.
.env.example has been out of date since the Redis migration - it still names REDIS_HOST and REDIS_PORT, which nothing reads any more.
Two git-tracked files under .vscode/ carry one developer's absolute paths, so the workspace settings only work on their machine.
ugly: src/controllers/orders.controller.ts is 902 lines with 11 handlers, sitting next to a src/services/ directory that holds exactly one file - the intent is visible and unfinished.
The same three-line catch block appears twelve times across the controllers, each logging slightly differently, while a central error middleware already exists to do it once.
A TODO at src/controllers/orders.controller.ts:511 reads 'remove before launch' and is dated 2024-03; the service launched two years ago.
prisma/migrations/ contains two migrations whose names describe the opposite of what they do (20250114_drop_index adds one), which makes the history unreadable at exactly the moment you need it.
